meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Success does not consist in never making blunders, but in never making the same one a second time'?
meta.ogDescription: Not George Bernard Shaw. It's from humorist Josh Billings (Henry Wheeler Shaw), first printed February 1872 — a case of mistaken 'Shaw.'

answer.label: Not George Bernard Shaw — actually Josh Billings
answer.sourceLine: This line was not written by George Bernard Shaw. As Quote Investigator ↗ documents, it originated with the 19th-century American humorist Josh Billings, whose real name was Henry Wheeler Shaw — and it first appeared in print in February 1872, decades before the modern “Shaw” mix-up. Billings wrote it in his trademark phonetic spelling: “Success don’t konsist in never making blunders, but in never making the same one the seckond time.”

source.excerpt: Success don’t konsist in never making blunders, but in never making the same one the seckond time.
trail: The saying is traced to humorist Josh Billings, first printed in February 1872, in Quote Investigator’s full investigation ↗.
“Josh Billings” was the pen name of Henry Wheeler Shaw (1818–1885) ↗, an American humorist second in fame only to Mark Twain in his day.
The shared surname “Shaw” is the likeliest root of the modern misattribution to the playwright George Bernard Shaw — a confusion Quote Investigator’s record does not support.
source.excerptNote: Billings deliberately used eccentric phonetic spelling; newspapers often standardized it on reprinting, which is how the smoothed modern wording — “Success does not consist in never making blunders…” — entered circulation.

author.name: Josh Billings (Henry Wheeler Shaw)
author.heading: About Josh Billings (Henry Wheeler Shaw)
author.bio: Henry Wheeler Shaw wrote under the pen name Josh Billings, dispensing folksy, aphoristic wit in a deliberately misspelled, phonetic style that delighted 19th-century readers. In the decades after the Civil War he was arguably America’s most popular humorist after Mark Twain, publishing best-selling collections and a long-running comic almanac. Many of his crisp maxims — later smoothed into standard spelling — still circulate today, frequently misattributed to more famous names.

misattribution.heading: How it ended up on George Bernard Shaw
misattribution.intro: The line is a genuine 19th-century American aphorism — but by the wrong Shaw. The famous playwright’s name is a magnet for polished, motivational sayings, and a shared surname did the rest.

items.why: Countless quote sites and business books pin this on the Irish playwright, but Quote Investigator ↗ finds no evidence he ever wrote or said it; its documented trail begins with Josh Billings in 1872.
The true author, Henry Wheeler Shaw ↗, shares a surname with George Bernard Shaw — and mid-20th-century reprints that credited only “H. W. Shaw” made the slide to the more famous Shaw easy.

Billings wrote it phonetically (“don’t konsist… the seckond time”); newspapers standardized the spelling and later versions swapped “blunders” for “mistakes” and “the second time” for “a second time,” producing the smooth modern line.

misattribution.truthLine: It’s a real Josh Billings maxim from February 1872, not a George Bernard Shaw quotation — per Quote Investigator ↗.

context.heading: A humorist's maxim, dressed up
lead: Josh Billings built his fame on plain-spoken, deliberately misspelled wit — the 19th-century equivalent of a viral one-liner. This saying is classic Billings: a tidy paradox about learning from failure, sharp enough to survive long after its author’s dialect spelling was scrubbed away.

Once the phonetic quirks were standardized and the byline shortened to “H. W. Shaw,” the line was easy prey for the internet’s habit of upgrading anonymous or half-remembered wisdom to a marquee name — here, the other, far more famous Shaw.
context.pull: A real aphorism, by the wrong Shaw.
